utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2010. I would like to greet the witness who is going to testify under oath in a few minutes. I would like to greet the accused, as well as all the counsels, all the members of the OTP, and everyone assisting us around the courtroom. I will give the floor to the Registrar, who has IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its objections to 4D and the Prosecution's list of documents tendered for admission via Witness Milivoj Petkovic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01216 and 01217 respectively. 3D and 4D has also submitted their objections to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered for admission via Witness Milivoj Petkovic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01218 and 01219 respectively. Furthermore, 4D has also submitted their response to Bruno Stojic's objections to their documents tendered for admission via Zdenko Andabak. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01220. 5D, 2D, 4D and the Prosecution has also submitted their list of documents to be tendered through Witness NO. These lists shall be given Exhibit IC01221, 01222, and, 01223 finally, 01224 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Witness, you may stand up, please. Could you please give us your name, first name, and date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mate Jelcic. The 4th of May, 1953, in Stubica, Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession or occupation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a law degree, and I'm currently retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, have you testified before a court of law on events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time that you're testifying before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I do know that you have a legal or law degree, but I'm going to give I was few explanations. You're going to answer questions that Mr. Coric's counsel is going to put to you based upon a written statement that you drafted and that you signed. Thereafter, other counsels may also put questions to you. The Prosecutor, who is on your right-hand side, as part of the cross-examination, may also put questions to you. And after that, if required, Mr. Coric's counsel may also ask some additional questions. The Judges before you may also ask you questions at any time based on your written statement or on the documents that will be put to you. Please try and be as precise as you can be in the answers that you will give to the questions put to you. You will see that when the Prosecutor asks questions, the way the questions will be put to you will be very different to those put to you by Mr. Coric's counsel or by the Judges because the Prosecutor is entitled to ask you very leading questions and he's entitled to give his point of view, which a Judge can't do. In this case, please listen carefully to the Prosecutor's question, and please try to keep your cool and answer the questions that are put to you. So there you go. This being said, I give the floor to Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jelcic. Could the witness please be provided with our binder with documents. Sir, could you please look at the first document, which is 5D0521. The first document, the following page, this is just a list of documents. You have the pink labels on the side. Mr. Jelcic, is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to read this statement in its totality?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] For the record, I would like to repeat the number. The number is 5D05112.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I have just one correction under 2, the month when I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us the exact date?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 4th of May, not on 4th of April. So it's the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the rest of your statement; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No. I have one more --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Slow down. I have told you, while I was preparing your testimony, when I start examining you, when I finish my question, count to 10 and then start giving your answer. Now, start answering, but before you do, count to 10.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Under number 6, the brigade police did not send reports to the duty operations room, but to the brigade, and that's the change that I would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what about the rest of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The rest of the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you were to testify before the Court about what is stated in your statement, would your testimony be identical to your statement, save for the two corrections that you've just made?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at your statement just briefly. Paragraph 3, under 3, that is, it says that from April 1992, you were a security officer in the Military Police Administration. Tell us, please, as a security officer, what did you do in the course of 1992, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: My duties were always connected with the Military Police Administration, the military police home, and as an officer I spent most of the time in the military police building. That's where I was in charge of security and other issues. I made sure that nothing was lacking. If something needed to be done, I was there to do it, and mostly in connection with the security issues and the supply issues. I made sure that nothing was at short supply. And as a security officer, I did not go into the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking about 1992. The witness told us what he did in 1993. And in 1992, what did you do, as a duty -- as a security officer?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The same thing. I was never sent into field. I was in charge of security in the main building and around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to your statement, under 7 and 8, I would just briefly like to hear from you whether you knew a person named Ante Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was he, and what did he do in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: In the 1993, Ante Prlic was the commander of the brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to him after 1993, after the war?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: After the war, he returned to his company, which was a gas station. That's where he had previously worked. He stole some money, quite a lot of money, from there, and then he left for Germany on a forged passport.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you about paragraph 10 of your statement, where you refer to Kreso Medic and Kresimir Tolj. Could you please look at the following document, which is P03613. In your statement, under 10, you stated that Kresimir Tolj could not appoint anyone to any function, and you also stated that Kreso Medic -- the document number is P03613. And you said that Kreso Medic carried out low-level tasks for the Ljubuski Military Police Centre as a delivery man and as a driver. Did you find the document?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And here you can see that a reference is made to the appointment of the prison warden in Otok, signed by Kresimir Tolj, and he appoints Kreso Medic as the prison commander. Did you find the document?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that -- I actually read out what you stated about Mr. Tolj and Mr. Medic. What would you be able to tell us about this appointment? Or, rather, do you have any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a comment. Kresimir Tolj could not appoint Kreso Medic in any way. The truth is that Kreso Medic did perform such duties in our main building, and here we see the number, but this is not a number from the Military Police Administration. "F-K" does not belong to the Military Police Administration. And in the upper right-hand side corner, the numbers have been corrected. Something has been done to them. I don't know what exactly. In any case, Kresimir Tolj was not in a position to appoint Kreso Medic to any position.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What did Kreso Medic do in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Menial jobs. If some spare parts were needed for the repairs of the water supply or the electricity, he would do that. He would be in charge of taking mail to the post and such things for the Military Police Administration; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And while you were the commander of the Military Police Centre in Ljubuski, can you tell us whether the Military Police Administration was housed in the same building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. I was looking at the document which is you are challenging. So should we draw from the document that this is a false document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the document is false or not, but this number is definitely not a number of the Military Police Administration. "F-K" was never used by the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand correctly, this person whom you knew, Kresimir Tolj, was a driver. He was just a driver, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Kresimir Tolj was not a driver. Kreso Medic was a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about Kresimir Tolj, then? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kresimir Tolj worked in the Crime Prevention Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he a rank-and-file soldier, a non-commissioned officer, or an officer of quite a high rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, at the time he did not hold a rank, at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer has not been recorded, and I asked you whether the Ljubuski Military Police Centre building also housed the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Military Police Administration was housed in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there every day? How often were you there, for how long? How many hours would you spend in the centre every day?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I would spend the whole day, all of my working hours, in the centre, unless another commitment took me elsewhere. But most of the time, I was there during the day, sometimes during the night when I was on duty. I was in charge of that building, and that's why I was there most of the time. I spent most of my time in the building, itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, in 1993, in that building see Ante Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No, never, I never saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, under 8, you say that Ante Prlic did not receive orders from the Military Police Administration or from the chief. Could you please look at the last document in your binder, which is P10190. This document was issued by the 4th Brigade Military Police, signed by Mr. Prlic, the gentleman that we have just spoken about, and it says in the document: "The command in Gabela is hereby requested to -- in accordance with the law and pursuant to an order issued by the head of the military police, Valentin Coric, for all detainees of Muslim ethnicity who are in possession of letters of guarantee to be released." You have just told us that Mr. Prlic did not receive orders from the chief of the Military Police Administration. However, we can see here that he is referring to an order given by the chief. How -- would you comment that?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: My comment would be as follows: It's the same situation as if some cleaning woman from one firm is calling upon the director of another firm for some services, asking him for some services. Well, it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you spoke about this in your statement -- just let me check the paragraph. In paragraph 9 of your statement, some letters of guarantee are mentioned here. What do you know about letters of guarantee? And it's also mentioned in this Prlic document, letters of guarantee. Did you hear about letters of guarantee in 1993? What do you know about the subject?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that in the summer of 1993, that letters of guarantee were arriving to a law firm in Ljubuski, and people would pick up letters of guarantee there that they used to leave the country, I assume. They would pick them up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did any such letters reach the Military Police Administration, or, rather, did you ever see a copy of a letter of guarantee or a letter of guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Never. No such letter ever arrived, nor did I ever see anything like that. And since I was in the Military Police Administration all the time, I can state that no letter of guarantee ever arrived there. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jelcic. Thank you, Your Honours. That completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about the counsel for Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the meantime, Witness, I would like to ask two follow-up questions. The first relates to the naming of Mr. Kreso Medic to head of Otok Military Prison. You said Mr. Kresimir Tolj was not competent to do that. I would like to know, if you know, what actually happened; whether, nevertheless, Kreso Medic did take control over Otok Military Prison or whether it was someone else. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I would know, because I know Kreso Medic and Kreso Tolj. Kreso Medic worked for me, he did work for me, so Kreso Medic could not go anywhere except where I told him to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your answer, then, if I understand correctly, would be, No, he did not become head of Otok Military Prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other question relates to the document P10190, which contains a certificate, as it is called, that Asim Obradovic and Zihno Obradovic ought to be transferred from Gabela to Ljubuski. Again, you told us that this order was not lawful. I would like you to tell me -- to tell the Bench whether, in fact, these persons were transferred to Ljubuski Military Prison or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, those persons weren't transferred to the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning, and good morning to everybody else in the courtroom, including you, Mr. Jelcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Petkovic Defence. In your statement and also today, you said that in 1992 you were an officer for security in the VP Administration. My question to you is this: Were you an officer of SIS or some other security service?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I was an officer of SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1993 were you also a SIS officer?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a SIS officer for a time, and then I was commander of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, are you certain that it was the SIS Service within the VP Administration and not a separate security service? Are you sure about that, absolutely certain?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the binder that you have before you, would you look for document 2D1501, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Just let me take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's the first document there in that set, but you can listen to me, listen to my question. Mr. Jelcic, this is a report by Ivica Lucic, as head of SIS, dated the 1st of December, 1993, sent to his new chief, who was Colonel Biskic at the time, forwarded to Colonel Biskic. And Ivica Lucic says in paragraph 2: "During the entire time of the war, there was a latent conflict between the military police and the Ministry of the Interior, the Main Staff, and also with the SIS Administration. Since some persons from the military police were involved in criminal activities, themselves, it was very difficult to work with them." And then a few paragraphs down, Ivica Lucic goes on to say: "When we wrote about this and said that co-operation between the VP Administration and the SIS was correct and proper, we primarily had in mind co-operation with Mr. Rado Lavric and a group of officers from the MP Administration. And I wish to contribute to join SIS and the military police closer together in that way too." Now, Witness, do you have any knowledge about the conflict that Mr. Ivica Lucic is writing about here?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about those clashes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in this security service within the MP Administration, did you have any knowledge about the problems that were ongoing with certain structures in Herceg-Bosna, the problems that the police had in co-operation with certain other structures in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jelcic, in paragraph 4 of your statement you speak about the military police establishment in 1992. And since you're a lawyer, yourself, in December 1992, let's analyse your statement and look at the documents that testify to that establishment. The documents we're going to discuss now are P957, and it's a document that you mention as being a document on the basis of which the organisation and establishment was conducted. It's the fifth document. But tell me first, have you ever seen this document before? Witness, I'm asking you. Have you ever seen the document before?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by Valentin Coric and Bruno Stojic. My question to you is this: The chief of the VP Administration and the head of the Defence Department, were they authorised to make decisions about the organisation and establishment of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to correct you. I'm not a lawyer -- THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something? Your Honours, I don't think it is proper to ask this witness what the authorisation and authority of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Let me repeat. I can't hear the translation in French. Mr. Coric, please repeat what you said. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I think it is improper to ask this witness about whether these people had the authority to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. I still can't hear the French. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Well, it's not my fault. It means that something is not working properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is because of the interpreters that I couldn't hear the French. It is better not to switch over systems, to avoid this kind of inconvenience. Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Well, never mind. I don't consider the question to be that important, so I'll just sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jelcic, let me correct myself. You are an administrative lawyer. You're not actually graduated from the Faculty of Law, but from the Higher School of Law; right? Can you answer that? Can we have an audible response, please?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: That's right, I'm not a graduate of the Faculty of Law and a lawyer in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question to you is this: According to your understanding of the regulations in Herceg-Bosna, who could make decisions about the establishment and organisation of the military police in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, except for this document, have you ever seen any rules and regulations, or a decision or order, on the establishment of the military police from December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I have seen documents, but I can't remember which ones exactly and how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said you saw one document?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I said I saw -- I did see something, but I can't remember what was in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether the document referred to MP organisation and establishment?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, why are you mentioning this document, then, in the context that I'm asking you about?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Which is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the context of the MP organisation. Why did you mention it; because it's a Valentin Coric document, or what's the importance of the document?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whose document it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's look at this document, and it's the only document which we have on MP organisation, dated December 1992. So let's take a look at parts of that document. But before we do that, tell me, if you know, whether the members of the military police were mobilised or were they taken into the military police service in some other way, were they admitted in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they weren't mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Witness, that in military units of the HVO, citizens were mobilised according to regular mobilisation procedure, whereas for the military police, people were admitted according to a special procedure?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they were admitted in the same way, admitted to the military police and to the HVO units in the same way, according to the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite clear on what you're saying. Were they mobilised into the military police then; is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, from the Defence Department, people would go to the military police, so they were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you say that the light assault battalions were exclusively combat units of the military police. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Therefore, they had exclusively combat assignments?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, combat and military police assignments, both.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: They had combat and military police assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, why, in your statement, did you say that they had exclusively combat assignments, whereas now you're testifying differently? Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I think what I'm saying is true and correct, and I think that's what I said over there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Pause there. Are you saying that you think you said the same thing in your statement; is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I don't think; I'm stating that they had combat and police duties. That's quite normal, to have both.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness -- tell us the military police tasks of the light assault battalions of the military police. Can you enumerate them, list them for us?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The MP Administration had five battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. Just list the military police tasks of the light assault battalions of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I can't list them because I don't know. I did other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, tell us, Witness, if you can, why, along with the regular military organisation of the HVO, why was a parallel system of combat units set up in the form of light assault MP battalions?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I said I don't know. I wasn't doing that kind of work, I wasn't in those units, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you know, could you tell us why those light assault units or, rather, combat units, were not subordinated to the Main Staff of the HVO, but were, rather, established within the framework of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were attached to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the document about the -- about the organisation of the military police. The document number is P957. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] First of all, can you hear me? Can anybody from the technical staff hear me at all? If not, could my microphone be made to work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] In principle, I'll say that I have an objection about this witness being asked questions that only the chief of the Military Police Administration or the highest-ranking officer in the Military Police Administration should answer, and not a person who is in charge of the maintenance of the Military Police Administration building. He made sure that all the cars were in their positions, that all the cars were parked, and so on and so forth. The questions put to him were about the duty of Mr. Stojic or myself, which is the minister or the chief of the administration respectively. I don't know how far that leads. Could you please protect this witness? Otherwise, he will go on answering, I don't know, I can't answer. And I would kindly request a short break to consult with my Defence counsel, and if that could be granted as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic, the witness said on several occasions that there were a number of things he knew nothing about. So rather than wasting time, maybe you could ask him whether he can address one or other subject. If he can't, move on to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am asking this witness based on his statement. If this witness says that all he knew was how to park vehicles in the parking-lot of the building, and that he doesn't know anything else, and that he doesn't know anything that is stated herein, I'm not going to have any questions for him. However, for as long as this statement exists in this courtroom, I believe that I have the right to question every sentence in the statement, and this is exactly what I'm doing. It is not my intention to discredit the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the document, at the very end on page 3, says that platoons of the military police attached to the brigades, the brigades. Could you please tell us, you have a degree in administrative law, how would you explain the word "pry," p-r-y? Why doesn't it say "in," "in brigades"?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, in your statement, you say -- or you speak about the battalions of the military police, and in paragraph 5 you say that military police battalion commanders reported to the duty operations room of the Military Police Administration and the commander of the operations zone. I am interested in reports sent to the commander of the operations zone. You said that you spent all days -- most of the days in the Military Police Administration building. My question is this: How do you know that the commanders of military police battalions reported to the commanders of the operations zones?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Madam, my office was very close to the operations duty room, and I heard. On several occasions, I heard those reports being sent, how they were being sent, where they were sent to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you heard that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise to my colleague Mr. Longone, but I think there's a very important matter that's come up which goes beyond the normal scope of objections and even for cross-examination. Based on what Mr. Coric said a moment ago, I think there's a fundamental question whether this witness has any foundation to be giving the testimony he's giving. The Chamber may recall - this has come up before - there has to be a foundation for a witness giving evidence. There has to be some basis of personal knowledge, there has to be something that makes it worthwhile -- excuse me, I'm getting a lot of interference from the other side. There has to be something, some measure, which makes it worthwhile for this Chamber to hear evidence from this witness on these points. According to what Mr. Coric just said -- according to what Mr. Coric just said, and I'm referring now to page 18 of the daily transcript: "In principle, I'll say that I have an objection about this witness being asked questions that only the chief of the Military Police Administration or the highest-ranking officer in the Military Police Administration should answer, and not a person who is in charge of the maintenance of the Military Police Administration building. He made sure that all the cars were in their positions, that all the cars were parked and so forth." Now, I put it to the Chamber that -- with respect, that that is a fundamentally different picture of the man and his position than what we have in the statement, in which he is described as, at some point, the head -- the commander -- at least in the English translation, as commander of the Military Police Centre in Ljubuski. Was he in the maintenance? With no disrespect intended for the gentleman, was he the commander of the police centre, with significant roles and responsibilities, and he can address policy and procedural questions, and fundamental structures and policies and reporting, or was he, again with respect, the maintenance man, parking cars? Now, this is more fundamental. This should not have to wait for cross-examination, because it may be that the witness, again with respect to the witness, we shouldn't receive this evidence at all. So until this is resolved -- and it's Mr. Coric who put this question into play, and I support him in that. This may or may not have been his intended result, but this is what Mr. Coric said. And until this is resolved, with great respect, we should not go forward with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once more, we are wasting time on procedural issues. I agree with Mr. Coric and with Mr. Scott. The essential question is: What exactly does this witness know? Ms. Alaburic, it might be better to determine, beforehand, what he knows and what he actually did, because if he was only in charge of the cars, there is no point in putting questions to him on the commander of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a point. I quite agree that this should be clarified. It should be clarified, I think, not at the expense of your time, actually. I think this is a special question. I would take it upon myself that you assert the level of knowledge and experience of this witness, as it were, at the expense of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, when I'm saying that we are wasting time, that's three people on their feet, all of that to no avail, because what I'm interested in, and this is something I must tell you, when the time comes to deliberate, it's not because you are all on your feet that this will change things. It is the statement of the witness and the exhibits that are shown, which is what we go by. You are going to object, and we are going to waste time. It might be more useful for the witness to tell us what he did exactly as the commander of the military police in Ljubuski. That is what is of interest. If he was looking after cars, fine, that we have understood. If he was involved in policy matters of the military police, that we have understood also. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that the witness's statement was not taken by Mr. Coric, but his Defence. Everything in the statement was said by the witness. The witness is being examined here pursuant to rules, and I believe that the key issue is where the witness was. He was in the Police Administration building. Witnesses can base their knowledge of the rules or what they saw and heard in different situations. The witness said just a minute ago that his office was only a few metres away from the operations duty room of the Military Police Administration, and that he heard a lot of things, that he saw a lot of things. The fact that the witness did not see a regulation and cannot interpret it does not mean that the witness doesn't know or that he didn't hear or see a certain thing. During the Prosecution case, we had witnesses who were shown combat reports, and they were illiterate, and still they could comment upon the combat reports. They were aware of some information in those combat reports, and that's what they testified about. He may not know the regulations, but the witness should be asked what he bases the information in his statement on. I asked him at the beginning what he did, and he said he was in charge of security and of the functioning of the entire centre. If he was in charge of security, then he obviously knew when the battalion commanders came and went. He also possibly knew how many members of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must tell you that my office is four metres away from the office of the President of the Tribunal. I don't know what the President of the Tribunal does. I have no idea. And my office is two centimetres away from Judge Mindua's office. I don't know what Judge Mindua does. It's not because the office is next-door that you know everything that's going on. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, and let me take the opportunity to say good morning to each of Your Honours, to the President. I regret if I'm trying your patience, Mr. President. I hope, after almost four years, the Chamber will hopefully believe that I don't rise to my feet unless I think it's something important. I do think this is an exceptional situation. I also want to clarify for the record that my objection, to the extent it was an objection, was not directed at Ms. Alaburic. It was directed more generally to the presentation of this witness. It may be through no fault of counsel for Mr. Coric. I don't know. I'm not throwing any stones in that direction, I'm not blaming anyone, but it very well could be and appears to be that a fundamentally false representation of this person has been put before the Court as a commander. When someone says they are a security officer, that doesn't mean custodian or maintenance man. When someone says they're the commander of the centre, after four years in a military case, we talk about commanders, generals, operational zone, brigade commanders, we don't talk about the head maintenance man at the building. And this is fundamental, and I go back, I think, to Judge Trechsel's point. I think it needs to be clarified before we take any further evidence on these points, because otherwise it may be of no value whatsoever. I regret if I've taken the time -- the Court's time unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be very short. I would simply say, with the greatest of respect, that we are wasting an awful lot of time with procedural issues. The weight and the utility of any testimony given by this witness will be evaluated by Your Honours once his evidence has been given, and it's completely open to the Defence and for the Prosecution to test the credibility and veracity and cogency of any testimony given by any witness in the box. Your Honours, Mr. Scott can do that and Ms. Alaburic can do that, but perhaps that can be done instead of delaying proceedings as they are being delayed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just support that, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do represent a different accused, and, therefore, I'm entitled to make my contribution. I, first of all, support what my learned friend Mr. Khan has said, and, secondly, simply observe that in light of the comment made a few minutes ago, a cross-examination which elicits the answer, I don't know, can often be extremely valuable cross-examination to that party and, in fact, in the way that Mr. Scott has indicated, to expose any weaknesses and perhaps get more quickly away from areas which are not worth exploring. Your Honour, not surprisingly, I entirely support the cross-examination of my learned friend lead counsel here and ask Your Honours to bear in mind that precisely that sort of cross-examination which elicits answers, I don't know, may be the most valuable cross-examination and use the time more effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell me what your exact position in Ljubuski was? What were you doing there? And then we will see what questions can be addressed during cross-examination. What were you doing, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in the military police building, and I was in charge of several things: maintenance; when there was training and when young policemen were involved, I made sure that they had equipment, that they were equipped; and that's the jobs I did. I made sure that the kitchen functioned, that the administration functioned, that everything functioned properly, so that the other people could work in the military police building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What else did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I did mostly, mostly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we understand things correctly, you were in charge of maintenance and of training of young policemen. That was, in essence, your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I prepared equipment for them. So when they turned up for training, they had everything they needed for that training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems to have been a misunderstanding. You were not training soldiers; you were just putting the chalk to write on the blackboard, for instance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no chalk involved in that, no chalk, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. But then perhaps it was sports material, weapons for manipulation, things like that, blind ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everything. Your Honour, everything they may have needed during training, I prepared all that for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua has a question pursuant to Rule 90 [as interpreted] ter (C) of our Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 92 [sic] ter, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Witness, this is an extremely important question, as the Prosecutor has reminded us of. I would like to know this: In your statement, which is document 5D05112, it says, in paragraph 3, that you were the commander of the Military Police Centre in Ljubuski. Can you very briefly give us the organisation chart of this centre with the position of the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police building was organised in this way: There was the Military Police Administration. There was also a school for young soldiers or, rather, military policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction on the transcript. I said "15 ter (C)," not "90." 15. Ms. Alaburic, you have seen and heard what the witness has said. Please adjust your questions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to go through your statement. I'm going to ask you what the source of your knowledge is. In paragraph 5, you refer to the fact that battalion commanders submitted daily, weekly, monthly reports, and, as needed, interim reports, first of all, to the duty operations room of the MP Administration and then, secondly, the commander of the operations zone. You go on to explain how the battalion commanders compiled their reports, where those reports went. You further speak about VP Administration reports which were sent to the Defence Department, and then Defence Department reports going to the government or, rather, to the HVO of the HZ-HB. Now, my question to you is: What is the source of your knowledge of what you describe in paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The source of my knowledge is that I knew everything on the basis of the duty operations room. I knew where the reports were going, who they were going to, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, did you work in that duty operations room?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No, but the room was close to mine. So when I didn't have -- when I wasn't doing other things, when I had a free moment, I would sit in the duty operations room, with the people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when it says that some police does something ex officio, do you know what that means, in the line of duty, in the line of their official duty?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, if the police is working in the line of duty, then they go about their police business, police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what the police is duty-bound to do under the law, not waiting for the government, the ministries, the Main Staff, or anybody else to tell them what they're supposed to do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Witness, what tasks the military police was obliged to do according to its line of duty, ex officio?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4 of your statement, Witness, towards the very end, you mention the reorganisation of the military police in mid-1993. And you mention a date there, and it's the 28th of July, 1993. I assume that's a mistake and that it should say the 28th of June, 1993. And you say that based on that order, assistant chief of the MP Administration was formed. Look at P2997 now, please. This is a piece of information sent by Valentin Coric to the command of the military police battalions, informing them about the reorganisation of the military police. Now, tell me, Witness, is that the document that you had in mind when you had the -- when you wrote the part of your statement that I just quoted from?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, apart from this document, did you see any other decision, regulation, or order relating to the new establishment of the military police in mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned the post of assistant chief of the VP Administration, and in this document it says, and I quote: "Pooling together the military police activities of the light assault battalion and military police battalion in the operative zone shall be conducted by the chief of the MP Administration for that zone that is authorised to command the battalions as well." Now, my question to you is as follows, based on that: The assistant chief of the MP Administration for the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina, is he authorised to command the 1st Light Assault Battalion and the 5th Battalion of the Military Police active in the area of that same operative zone?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, P3487, which is a decision by the head of the Defence Department, dated the 16th of July, 1993. And as assistant chief of the MP Administration for the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina, Zlatan Mijo Jelic is being appointed to that post. And I'm going to show you a few more documents first, and then I'm going to ask you my question later. The next document, P4146, P4146. It is an order from Valentin Coric, dated the 12th of August, 1993, in which, in the attachment, it says, and I quote: "The chief of the MP Administration conveyed most of his authority to the assistants for the individual operations zones." And so, for example, in the -- for the chief of the military police of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina, Zlatan Mijo Jelic was appointed. Several further lines down, it says the assistant chiefs of the MP Administration received an order and authorisation from the chief of the Military Police Administration to establish and organise, in each of the four operational zones, military police light assault battalions, and to reorganise the existing battalions of the general and traffic military police. Just a moment, I'll read on. The next document is P3778. A little patience, please, and I'll come to my question after we've looked at that document. It is an order from Valentin Coric, dated the 28th of July, 1993, in which it says, and I quote: "The assistant chiefs are duty-bound, in addition to engaging in combat, the military police and their re-subordination to the commander of the HVO or to the commander of the corresponding zones specifically authorised by the commander of the HVO." This order was sent to the following addressees, or, rather, four assistant chiefs of the VP Administration for the operative zone. Now, Witness, under this column "Delivered to," is it true that the order was sent to the assistant chiefs of the VP Administration in the four operative zones?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Excuse me, Counsel. Again, Your Honour, I apologise if I annoy the Chamber with this, but I don't think the issue's been resolved. It doesn't matter how many documents Ms. Alaburic reads to the witness. She can read documents to him all day long. She just put four documents in a row without a question, four documents, to the maintenance man at the centre. This witness, with great respect, has no competence -- he has no basic, fundamental foundational-level competence to address these questions, and we can read documents to him all day long. I can stand up and read documents to him and ask for him to give opinions. There's no value to this, Your Honour, with great respect. There is no value to receiving this evidence from this witness. He can't talk about the policies and structures and how the military police was organised, because he parked cars in the parking-lot. The Chamber needs to -- with great respect, needs to address this more fundamentally. Otherwise, we are, indeed, wasting time in taking the evidence of an incompetent witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I'd just like to ask Mr. Scott for a little patience. I took on board what was said about the examination of this witness, and I'm not going to ask him about these documents. I'm going to show him one more document -- or, rather, two more documents, and then I'm going to ask a question of fact, about fact, which I consider to be extremely important in this trial. And I think I have eight more minutes to do that in, and I will stick to the time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I apologise for interrupting my good friend Ms. Alaburic, who I have great respect and affection for, but I don't understand. What's the point of raising four documents which she's not going to ask questions about them. She just said: "I'm going to show him one more document. I'm not going to ask him about these documents." Why do we spend court time talking about documents we're not going to examine on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Ms. Alaburic has six minutes left. She will finish in six minutes. If she's wasted our time, it's just too bad. It's her problem. Please go ahead, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, Witness, is P5869, 5869. This is an excerpt from the minutes of a meeting held in the Military Police Centre in Ljubuski, held on the 10th of October, 1993. It is a regular monthly meeting of the heads of -- or leading officers of the Military Police Administration with the military police battalion commanders, and here, of those listed present, we see that Zlatan Mijo Jelic was present as assistant chief for the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina. In view of the fact that the meeting was held in Ljubuski, at the MP Centre there, do you remember the meeting, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I remember a number of meetings being held. I can't remember this particular one, but there were several such meetings with the same people attending.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see, with the same people attending. Now, did, for example, Mr. Ivan Ancic attend those meetings, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Ivan Ancic was there. I don't know if he was there every time, but he did attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about Zlatan Mijo Jelic, Witness. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did Zlatan Mijo Jelic come to those meetings, for example, in the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next document is 4D2063, 4D2063, which is a proposal from Valentin Coric, dated the 11th of November, 1993, sent to Perica Jukic, and, among other things, saying that the duties of the assistant chiefs of the MP Administration for the Mostar Military District be relieved of duty -- rather, that Zlatan Mijo Jelic be relieved of duty. Now, do you know that towards the end of 1993, Zlatan Mijo Jelic ceased to be the assistant chief of the MP Administration for the Military District of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that the Military Investigative Prison of Ljubuski, or remand prison, began operating in September 1993. Today, you corrected some of the information in your statement, but you did not correct that piece of information, so I'm going to ask you whether you stand by the fact that the Ljubuski Prison was set up in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at P373 - yes, P373 - which is the house rules of the prison in Ljubuski passed on the 7th of August, 1992. And it is signed by the assistant chief of the VP Administration for Military Investigative Affairs. Tell us, Witness, did you know about these house rules, the existence of these house rules?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But these house rules date to 1992. Can you explain to us how come we have house rules for 1992, and you say that the prison in Ljubuski was established a year later, in September 1993, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The prison existed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now look at the last document, P956, 956, which is a report from the military police for 1992. And in the first part, it talks about the work of the individual services, and what I'm interested in and would like to focus on are prisons. And it says here that by the end of June 1992, three military remand prisons were formed in Mostar, Ljubuski, and Livno, and that in July 1992, a fourth military remand prison was set up in Capljina. Tell us, Witness, to the best of your knowledge, is that data correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. And good morning, sir. We have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 2D.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions, in principle, for this witness, but I want to correct a lack of precision in the transcript, to put that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jelcic -- this is page 16, line 24 of today's transcript, but it's not important as far as you're concerned. When Ms. Alaburic asked you about the mobilisation of the military police, you said that they were those coming from the Defence Department. That's what was recorded. Did you mean the Administration for Defence or Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I meant Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did mobilisation go via the Administration for Defence or the Department for Defence?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Department for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have some 15 minutes of cross-examination, but it will all depend on what the witness's first answer is to my question, what he's going to say first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, and then we'll have the break and the Prosecutor will do the cross-examination. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I represent the Praljak Defence, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. Your statement, the one you confirmed as being your statement here this morning, in paragraph 4, the third paragraph reads as follows: "Besides the active VP force, there was also the brigade VP, which was a constituent part of the brigade, like all other units of that brigade." Now, my question is as follows: Is that your statement -- or, rather, do you stand by that assertion and statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Then, tell me, how do you know that? How do you come to know that a military police platoon is exactly the same thing as all the other platoons of the brigade military police? On what grounds are you able to say that and do you know that? Explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the platoons were the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My colleague tells me that my question was wrongly recorded, so I'm going to repeat it. My question was: How come you know that that is so, that the platoons in the brigades, all of them were exactly the same, regardless of whether it was a military police platoon or some other platoon? How do you know that? What is the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. I didn't understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is a mistake? Now I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a mistake that all platoons are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. That means -- or, rather, you tell me. Does that mean that this statement of yours, in paragraph 4, third paragraph, is not correct? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness didn't say in his statement that all the platoons were the same. What he says was that the brigade platoon was within the composition of the brigade or a constituent part of the brigade, like all other units of that brigade, which means that it was a constituent part of the brigade. He didn't say whether they were all the same, or different, or equal. He said that they were just a constituent part of the brigade, like all other units of that brigade. That's what -- how the statement reads. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, that's the way this is being interpreted, but I'm going to ask the witness -- let me repeat for the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, if my learned friend would just allow me. Page 38, line 3, the English interpretation of what the witness is saying in court today is: "I think the platoons were the same everywhere." Now, whether that does or doesn't need some further exploration or explanation in questions, it's no use Mr. Coric's counsel tells us what his statement said, because he said, I think the platoons were the same everywhere, and the simple understanding of that is what he says. If he means something different then, well, I invite anybody to explore it, if they wish to, but that's what it says there on the transcript in English. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The witness answered the question, thus I drew Mr. Kovacic's attention to the fact that the witness misheard him because Mr. Kovacic made a mistake in his question. You can see it on page 37, lines from 23 through 25. He asks: [In English] "... to know that the military police platoon is exactly the same thing as all the other platoons of the brigade military police?" "Of the brigade military police." [Interpretation] Which means that the question, the way it was put to him, was whether the military police platoon was the same as all the other platoons of the brigade military police, and that's why I asked my learned friend to correct himself, because it was really not clear what he was asking him. It turns out -- or he interpreted the question as being asked to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was corrected. I'm not going to dwell upon mistakes and interpretations thereof. I'll repeat my question, because obviously the witness doesn't understand what he said, what he's saying, so I'll go over the same grounds as an elementary school witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, concentrate to what you're saying. In your statement, it says literally -- and you signed this statement, and you confirmed earlier today that this was, indeed, your statement. It says as follows: "Besides the active VP force, there was also the brigade VP, which was a constituent part of the brigade, like all other units of that brigade." This is your statement. My question is this, my first question: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I know that because I was in Ljubuski. I know exactly how things were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever at the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, let's go on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind and repeat the answer. It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me approximately how many times, when did you go to the brigade command, and how often could you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: It was not often. But since I hail from Ljubuski, I had a lot of acquaintances in the brigade. That's why I popped over to the brigade now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us who the commander of the brigade in Ljubuski was?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: There were several commanders. At that time, it was Cane Primorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What do you know by "then"? Cane Primorac was the commander when?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: I believe in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at that time in 1993, or for the most part of 1993, who was the commander of the brigade platoon of the military police in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade platoon in 1993 was Ante Prlic for a while, and I believe that he was replaced by somebody called Bebic. That's -- during that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember who, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry. At page 40, line 17, we got a question which, in English, is distinct the ambiguous, as recorded on the transcript: "Okay. Were you ever at the brigade commander?" Now, there are two possible questions there: Were you ever at the brigade command or, Were you ever the brigade commander? Now, I've got some recollection of what it was that Mr. Kovacic asked, but as it stands on the transcript, and therefore it is important to make sure that it's right, as it stands on the transcript it's completely unclear, in English, what that question was. And actually, as it happens, it doesn't appear that the answer that I've got at line 21, "Yes, I was at the brigade," doesn't appear to be a direct answer to either question, actually, in whatever form. So, really, there is confusion here, and I'm just inviting it to be cleared up one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, could you perhaps ask for clarification regarding this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the interpretation problem or inadequate terminology that we use in Croatian as opposed to what we use in English; hence, such situations which we need to clarify. But maybe you can give me three or four more minutes, because this is a linguistic problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, when I ask you whether you were ever at the command of the brigade, did you understand that as the brigade offices? Could you please answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade offices, as visiting the brigade offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did not understand my question as me asking you whether you were a member of the command?

utterances.speaker: MATE JELCIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this clarifies the matter. This is a linguistic problem. Very well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as I am concerned, it's clear, but perhaps you can help me. Could you please tell us, what your commander, who were you reporting to directly? Who was your superior, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, when you were reporting -- when you were drafting reports, you would be reporting directly to Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this is a good time for the break, or I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's better for you to complete your cross-examination. You have a few minutes left, so it's better for you to complete your cross-examination now, before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was forced to waste some time on my colleague's questions, which was not my intention. I think it would only be fair for me to be given time after the break. That would relieve pressure and we would save time, because the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you like. We'll have the break now, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak's Defence counsel. Yes, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the break I consulted with Mr. Coric, and I informed the Prosecutor's office thereof, and the matter is this: During the examination earlier today, the witness provided different information than he did during the preparation for his testimony, what he said to the Coric Defence. The witness has serious health problems. I don't know what the reason for his change of testimony is. However, given the new circumstances, after the consultation with Mr. Coric, we would like to give up on this witness. We would like to withdraw his statement. I have spoken about that with the OTP, and Mr. Scott understands our position and does not object to the withdrawal of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That a right you are fully entitled to. I shall turn to my colleagues to see whether they agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber notes that you are withdrawing this witness. Sir, I thank you for having come to testify, but you have understood that Mr. Coric's Defence counsel is withdrawing your statement. She is fully entitled to do so. I thank you for having come, and I wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I can just add one thing on the name of the Chamber. We've heard that you have health problems, and we wish you the best for a recovery of your health.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to throw in this note yet again. Well, I'm not sorry. I'd like to be courteous, but I'm not saying I'm sorry, actually. Your Honour, we don't accept that the Coric Defence is simply entitled to withdraw this evidence. We don't accept that. It's -- once a witness has come along and he's given evidence, we contend they're not in that position. And, Your Honour, we would really like just a brief opportunity to consider whether our position, the Petkovic Defence, is that we simply assent to that without any argument at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could interrupt. Your Honours, I do apologise to my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, but perhaps if there is any more discussion on this issue, it would be better for it to be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will ask the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we just move into private session just briefly? I would like to provide some information about the health condition of the witness, because I see that everybody needs additional information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into closed session. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very briefly, we have taken advantage of those few minutes to consider the position in the Petkovic Defence. Your Honour, although we maintain our position of principle that there is no entitlement to withdraw, in this particular case we don't oppose that course, having had the opportunity to considered the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no problem anymore. Since there is no problem anymore, would you like to say something, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is an entitlement, and they exercised it. And, of course, on the other hand, none of the testimony that we heard, or the documents that were introduced through the witnesses -- through this witness, can be used, so there's no prejudice to anyone else. Normally, you would ask that the record be stricken, although it's an impossibility to strike a record, but I think that's the point that I wanted to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow -- I'd like to thank you all for having taken the floor. Is tomorrow's witness available? If that is the case, we could perhaps save some time. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because I could not have envisaged this happening. I didn't know that proceedings would take this course today. But, yes, he is ready to come into court tomorrow. There's no problem about tomorrow. The next witness is ready tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In that case, we'll wait until tomorrow and resume our hearing at 9.00 tomorrow morning, since we are sitting in the morning. I would like to thank you all. Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to make, something I noticed over the past few days. For example, specifically Ms. Alaburic is using terms which are not customary in the Croatian Defence Council and Croatian Army. So, for example, she refers to disciplinary rules instead of saying "stegovnik," and then she uses another term for re-subordination and attachment which is unusual, and I noticed some new terms being used today. If this practice continues, of course, this language is B/C/S, as somebody has termed it - I don't mind - but if this continues I'm going to ask for interpreters for my own witnesses for certain terms, because I'd like somebody to show me, in military terminology, or a piece of paper in any language, where it says "spontano pretpocinjavanje" or "spontaneous re-subordination." We have heard talk about disciplinary measures as being "stegovni pravilnik," "stegovni sud," a disciplinary court, et cetera, so these terms and other terms are some that my witnesses did not understand. So in future, if something like that happens, would you please allow me to stand up and intervene, objection? I'm going to avail myself of the right to get up on my feet and object. And this has happened in dozens of cases. I have mentioned just the most important. But in future, I shall be on my feet and complain and object to every term that was used. And you know what the interpretation is like here anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I deem it necessary to respond. I don't wish to react to what one of the accused says, but I assume that you can't understand the substance of the objections made by Mr. Coric because you are hearing the same words in interpretation. What Mr. Coric wants to say to me is this: that I don't use the real Croatian language, the proper Croatian language, but that my language is something that is closer to the B/C/S variant, and that for that reason he and his witnesses will, in future, need an interpreter for themselves to interpret what I am saying. I could talk to you at great length about a pure Croatian variant of the language, or Croatian language -- the Croatian language as understood by some people, and about the Croatian language which contains words originating from the Serbian language, from the Turkish language, and which we consider to be the richness of both the Croatian language and every other language of the former Yugoslavia, and I'll tell you why I frequently use certain linguistic variations which are closer to the Serbian language.
