I use them when I know that our interpreters are also from the Serbian linguistic area and that it will be simpler for them if I say -- I use the Latin term in saying "December," for the month of December, instead of "Prosinac," which would be in the pure Croatian language, because I want to avoid any difficulties to the interpreters in interpreting. In my own country, I use all the linguistic variants of the Croatian language, and I shall continue to use them in this courtroom. And if I consider that a certain expression taken from the Serbian language or the Bosnian language is better suited to expressing what I want to say, I shall use that language. And if this is something that Mr. Coric and his witnesses don't like, then I'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether separate interpreters are needed to interpret my multi-ethnic Croatian language to be translated into the language spoken by Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I have spoken up here for the purpose of protecting my witnesses. I'm not here as an interpreter and to be played up to -- by anyone in this courtroom. Let me put Ms. Alaburic right. The term "cisti Hrvatski jezik," "pure Croatian language," does not exist, except perhaps in your terminologies. There's the -- what does exist is the official language of Croatia, which is the Croatian literary language, which must be spoken officially by all officials in the state service, on state television, and so on. But people are free to speak any way they like, but I asked to be protected from her terms that my witnesses do not understand, some of them. Now, if you thought you would provoke me or my witnesses by using those terms that you use, you're not going to. I lived in all three republics of the former Yugoslavia. Macedonia, and we understood each other in Macedonia, so don't try and do the dirty business on me and say that I have been saying something that I have not. The fact that what I'm saying and my speech is provoking such emotional reaction on your part is not my fault. I just wanted to protect my witnesses, because you are confusing the witnesses. Perhaps you're provoking them intentionally in that way. But I know the people. You can't provoke them. They're quite okay, these people. Thank you, Your Honours, and I'm going to be persistent, I'm going to rise to my feet, every time you use terms that I never read in any literature, in any book, and that come from a language where I can assume -- a language which I can assume that my witnesses don't understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your counsel, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to say the following: I can't speak in the name and on behalf of Mr. Coric. He got on his feet himself. But I can say something with respect to this discussion from the Coric Defence. And as I understood Mr. Coric's intention, it was not to insult Ms. Alaburic or the way in which she speaks, or any of the -- neither do any members of the Coric Defence consider that Ms. Alaburic and anybody else in the courtroom speaks a language that they ought not to be speaking. I'm sorry if she has understood it that way. I see that she has taken it to heart, but I don't think she understood what Mr. Coric said. As far as I understood him, he wanted to say this: His witnesses were in the army or the military police at a time when certain names and titles were used to refer to these things. Of course, there are synonyms for these same things used in the former Yugoslavia and which are still used to the present day. But he is afraid that if the witnesses are not asked a question using the exact name and title of what was used and term that was used when they were in service, they won't understand what is meant. I think that that was his objection, and it wasn't his aim to insult Ms. Alaburic. I'm very sorry that this is happening in this courtroom, and I would like to apologise if in any way she thought that we wanted to insult her in any way. I'm very sorry if that is the case, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned friend. Your Honours, I thought we had the good fortune to finish a little bit early today, and however interesting the etymological and linguistic presentations have been, it may not be the most efficient use of court time. A couple of solutions come to mind. The first, of course, is that it must be right that every counsel has the full discretion to use the words that counsel deems appropriate. Any uncertainty or clarification can be elicited from a witness in re-examination. And, indeed, if Mr. Coric has concerns, there is a procedure in this jurisdiction of proofing, and in proofing it's always open, prior to the witness coming to the box, for the witness to be told that these terms may be used, this is what these terms mean, and that may be a time-saving measure. Your Honours, I would simply urge that this is all to do about nothing, we don't waste more time. If Mr. Coric still, despite these other avenues that are available, has concerns, perhaps it could be made in writing and it could be ruled upon in the normal manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I wish to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber is not going to watch over this ping-pong game. This is a way of abusing the Trial Chamber's time, so we will let you know what our point of view is on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should clarify, on a factual level, whether we're dealing with a personal attack by Mr. Coric against me or is it a question of principle, a request of principle. In this courtroom, we have counsel who do not speak the Croatian version of the Croatian language, and nobody ever raised this question and asked whether the witness would understand the language they're speaking, or witnesses who don't speak Croatian at all but are speaking their own Bosniak language. We also have a situation and situations in which my colleagues from the Defence counsel and from the Prosecution, who are foreigners, speak their own language and are translated into B/C/S, interpreted into B/C/S, very often by interpreters who come from the Serbian area, so we get interpretations into the Serbian language. Nobody ever raised this issue. Nobody ever asked whether the witnesses understand this Serbian language or not. Thirdly, no witness, including Mr. Coric's witnesses, ever told me that they don't understand a word that I have uttered in my questions. Therefore, Mr. Coric has absolutely no factual basis for presenting the allegations that he has presented. What Mr. Coric said I consider to be a direct personal attack against me. I consider that it is completely unfounded, and I would like you to seek ways and means to ensure that the conduct of Mr. Coric should be commensurate to the type of conduct that is suited to a courtroom of this kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, please sit down. I'm going to say something. As far as I'm concerned, no one is attacking anyone. It's just that a Defence counsel of a particular accused would like the witnesses to be able to speak in their own language, i.e., the Croatian language, as Mr. Coric has said. It so happens that this is an ongoing topic before this Tribunal. This is something we have addressed already. We have already talked about the use of B/C/S. The response provided by the administration, i.e., the Registrar of this Tribunal, runs as follows: There are a series of interpreters who are familiar with B/C/S. I had asked -- because I have been involved in another case and I was confronted with the same problem, I thought innocently that when there is a Serbian, it is better that the interpreter is Serbian; when there is a Croatian witness, it's better that the interpreter is Croatian; and when it's a Bosnian, it is better that the interpreter speaks a language of Sarajevo. I was told that things did not happen that way because the interpreters were supposed to use all the linguistic variants. So it depends on the schedule, and that is how the interpreters are allocated to various cases. This is what the administration of this Tribunal responded. I believe Mr. Khan is quite right when he says that a solution can be found during the redirect. When Mr. Coric's Defence realises that there is a problem, there is still time to come back and address the wrong term that has been used. Let me take the case of my own language, which is spoken in Canada, which is spoken in African countries, which is spoken in Belgium and so on. Sometimes I don't understand a term. I don't understand what a Canadian is saying when he comes from Quebec, because the terms he uses are terms which I'm not familiar with. I assume the same thing happens in your language. I understand perfectly. It's better when the word is perfectly well understood by the witness and the witness is perhaps speaking a language which is somewhat different from the language used by the person putting the questions. As Mr. Khan has said, and he is absolutely right, there is a way of finding a solution to this; for instance, the issue of the proofing. If, before the testimony, the counsel says to the witness, This is a topic that is going to be addressed, these are the types of questions that my be raised, these are the terms that will be used, do we agree on the use of such and such a term, then a solution can be found. But during redirect, if there are diverging views, this can be corrected at that time. It so happens that the Judges have the documents before them, and they have translations which are worth what they are worth. But if a Judge realises that there might be a problem, then the Judge will put the question even if sometimes we are told we ask too many questions. As far as the term of re-subordination is concerned, if I realise that it is not very clear and what the witness is saying is not very clear, then I will tell the witness, What does "re-subordination" mean to you, and then he will answer the question. So we do have solutions at hand. If Mr. Coric wants to take the floor and say that he had rather have a Croatian interpreter, I would tend to agree with him, but it so happens that the administration of this Tribunal doesn't operate that way. So we are all doing our best, and I would like to state that one must not imagine that some teams are attacking other teams, because I'm sure that everyone has one single objective, which is to establish the truth. We shall meet tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
